text: What do our experiments say about accuracy, model size, and inference cost?

Target duration: about 1 minute(s).

Open with the central question. This talk reports completed experiments and the limits of what they show. The Cora run was an early implementation check; the main comparisons now use ogbn-arxiv.
A brief reset before the results
Built three-seed full-graph, random, and degree references.
Compared edge selection, teacher strength, KD, and inference cost.
Current evidence is centered on ogbn-arxiv; Cora remains a project milestone, not a main result.

Target duration: about 1 minute(s).

This slide reorients listeners who saw the earlier proposal. We used Cora to check the pipeline, then moved to ogbn-arxiv for the experimental comparisons. Since then, we completed old-teacher and larger-teacher student experiments, and measured sparse-model inference.
The teacher provides guidance; the sparse student tests whether that knowledge survives compression
Learns from the original graph and produces edge scores and softened class probabilities.
Uses fewer graph connections and a smaller model while learning the same node-classification task.
Does teacher guidance help the compressed student preserve accuracy better than labels alone?

Explain the actual motivation for the teacher–student design. The full-graph teacher supplies two possible forms of guidance: edge sensitivity scores and softened output probabilities. The sparse, smaller student is then compared with a matched student trained only from labels. The project asks whether teacher guidance preserves accuracy under graph and model compression.
Each result maps back to one question
How much accuracy can we retain as we remove graph edges?
Does teacher-guided edge selection beat simple selectors?
Does knowledge distillation help the sparse student?
Do sparsity and a smaller model reduce measured inference cost?

Introduce the four questions that organize the results: accuracy under edge removal, teacher-guided selection versus simple selectors, whether KD helps the sparse student, and measured inference savings from sparsity and a smaller model.

Target duration: about 3 minute(s).

Walk left to right. The teacher sees the original graph. For edge scoring, the implementation adds one scalar gate for each undirected connection, holds teacher parameters fixed, and differentiates the training-node cross-entropy through the edge weights. The absolute gate-times-gradient score ranks connections. We retain the top K to form one sparse graph. The student then trains on that graph. In KD mode, the frozen teacher's softened probabilities are also targets. This score is a one-shot sensitivity calculation, not an edge-gate network trained over epochs.
The larger teacher creates room for a smaller student
Model capacity is part of the compression question
The width-128 student has about 5.1× fewer parameters than the stronger teacher.
The width-64 ablation tests whether edge removal is needed when model size itself can shrink.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

The student is smaller relative to the stronger teacher, not relative to the original width-128 teacher. That distinction matters. The original teacher has 21,672 parameters and the stronger teacher has 110,120. Our main student remains width 128, while the width-64 ablation tests model-size reduction separately. The 67.55% and 71.86% teacher accuracies are three-seed means from the full graph.

Teacher parameters are frozen; the student is optimized by backpropagation.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

Explain the separation carefully. First, compute edge sensitivity once from the frozen teacher. This produces scores; we do not optimize every gate repeatedly. Second, select the fixed budget. Third, train the student. In CE mode the student uses labels only. In KD mode it combines cross-entropy with temperature-scaled KL divergence. The teacher's predictions are precomputed, and the optimizer updates only student weights.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

Every main pruning method uses the same graph budget and split. The full grid uses three seeds and three edge-removal levels for the major methods. For teacher-guided pruning, CE and KD students share the exact selected connectivity. The width-64 control and the KD hyperparameter sweep answer narrower questions and should not be mistaken for full three-seed results.
Quality, runtime, and memory answer different questions
Report model quality and system cost together
Test labels used only for final reporting
CE/KD use same graph and width
Timing uses warm inference with graph data already on the GPU; setup and preprocessing are separate.

Target duration: about 1 minute(s).

Accuracy answers whether the model predicts well. Latency and memory answer whether inference becomes cheaper on the measured hardware. We used an NVIDIA A30, with ten warm-up runs and thirty measured runs, with graph data already on the device. Validation supports model selection; test accuracy is reserved for reporting. This is a controlled benchmark, not a claim about every deployment system.

title: Three-seed mean test accuracy by selector

text:
Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

At 20% edge removal, degree pruning retains essentially the full-graph accuracy in this three-seed mean: 67.62% versus 67.55%. At 60% removal, the model loses about 2.98 percentage points. This answers the first question with a tradeoff curve, rather than claiming edge removal is free. The random baseline is part of the comparison grid; the current strongest reference is degree pruning.

Original teacher: KD trails matched CE at every edge budget
Teacher-guided students · 2-layer width-128 student · three-seed mean test accuracy
KD underperforms the same student trained with labels alone.
Degree remains the strongest selector in the tested grid.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

This is the first teacher-guided result. Both student objectives use the same teacher-selected graph and the same width-128 architecture. With the original teacher, KD is lower than CE by about 1.5 to 1.6 percentage points across the three budgets. Degree-based pruning also remains stronger than teacher-guided CE. This motivates asking whether teacher quality explains the weak KD transfer.

Sources: PROJECT_PLAN.md and experiment artifacts under runs/ (main grid, strong_teacher_grid, and kd_sweep40_seed0 as relevant).
Why we trained a larger teacher
The original teacher may not have provided sufficiently strong distillation targets
A stronger source may help KD, but its offline and inference costs also rise.

Target duration: about 1 minute(s).

The original two-layer width-128 full-graph teacher averaged 67.55% test accuracy. The larger three-layer width-256 BatchNorm teacher averaged 71.86%, a 4.31 point increase. It also has about 5.1 times as many parameters and 3.2 times the median inference latency. We ran the follow-up because the original teacher's KD student lagged behind CE, and teacher quality could be one reason. The experiment tests that explanation; it does not assume the larger model will solve KD.

Sources: PROJECT_PLAN.md and experiment artifacts under runs/ (main grid, strong_teacher_grid, and kd_sweep40_seed0 as relevant).
Stronger teacher: KD improves, but CE still leads
Three-seed mean test accuracy on teacher-guided sparse graphs
Yet strong-teacher KD remains 0.33–0.71 pp below matched CE.
RQ3 answer so far: a better teacher helps, but KD still does not beat CE.

Target duration: about 3 minute(s).

The stronger teacher improves teacher-guided KD over the old-teacher KD by 1.50, 1.47, and 1.15 percentage points at 20, 40, and 60 percent removal. This supports the idea that teacher quality mattered. However, KD remains below its matched CE student by 0.33, 0.39, and 0.71 points, and degree pruning remains the strongest selector. We should therefore say stronger teachers help transfer but do not establish that KD improves this sparse student.

Sources: PROJECT_PLAN.md and experiment artifacts under runs/ (main grid, strong_teacher_grid, and kd_sweep40_seed0 as relevant).
Prior work points to possible bottlenecks
These findings motivate checks; they do not identify the cause of our KD gap

Prior saliency methods struggled to beat random when pruning graph connections alone. This motivates testing our teacher-loss ranking against matched-budget selectors; it is not a direct evaluation of our score.

DGKD identifies fixed coupling between target-class and non-target-class signals in a common graph-KD objective. Its adaptive weighting improved MLP students, suggesting that the transfer objective is worth examining.
Our results cannot yet separate an edge-selection effect from a KD-loss effect.
[1] Wang et al., “Pruning graph neural networks by evaluating edge properties,” KBS 256 (2023), 109847. doi:10.1016/j.knosys.2022.109847
[2] Tian, Xu & Li, “Decoupled graph knowledge distillation,” Neural Networks 179 (2024), 106567. doi:10.1016/j.neunet.2024.106567

Context from prior work: (1) Wang et al. report that saliency metrics can struggle to beat random when pruning only graph adjacency; their methods differ from our teacher-loss edge score. (2) Tian et al. diagnose coupling in a classical graph-KD objective and propose DGKD with adaptive weighting; this motivates, but does not prove, an objective issue in our experiment. The current EdgeTrim-KD experiments do not isolate edge selection from loss choice. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2022.109847 ; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2024.106567
Temperature 2 led the seed-0 validation sweep
40% removal · only alpha and temperature changed · one seed
Exploratory only: validation gain is small, and the top settings still need confirmation across seeds.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

This is a 12-run seed-0 sweep at 40 percent removal. Temperature 2 gave the best validation result at each tested alpha, and temperature 4 was consistently weaker. The top validation setting was alpha 0.75, T 2 at 66.90%, versus 66.61% for the seed-0 CE control. The difference is small and this is one seed; do not treat it as a final KD win. The test score is not used for tuning.

A direct reminder that edge count and model capacity both matter
Width-64 KD is 1.54 pp below CE; unpruned width 64 also beats the width-128, 40%-pruned CE result.

preview: Configuration | Test acc. | Latency | Peak memory | Params

text:
Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

This focused width-64 ablation uses seed 0, so do not treat it as a three-seed result. Unpruned width 64 has 66.75% accuracy, 11.86 ms latency, and 1.46 GiB memory. The width-64 teacher-graph CE student has 64.32%, 8.34 ms, and 0.98 GiB. The width-64 KD version drops to 62.78% and is slower at 9.77 ms, with the same memory. The width-64 unpruned model also exceeds the width-128 40%-pruned CE result in accuracy while using less latency and memory. This makes model capacity a key control.

Sources: PROJECT_PLAN.md and experiment artifacts under runs/ (main grid, strong_teacher_grid, and kd_sweep40_seed0 as relevant).
More edge removal reduces latency and memory
Sparse student profiles on the A30 · mean across CE and KD runs and three seeds
60% removal: about 49% lower latency and 50% lower peak inference memory than the full-graph reference.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

These measurements show actual hardware behavior, not an assumption that fewer edges always means proportional speedup. The full-graph reference is 18.91 milliseconds and 2.72 GiB. Sparse-student averages are 15.73, 12.61, and 9.68 milliseconds at 20, 40, and 60 percent removal, with memory of 2.26, 1.81, and 1.35 GiB. One 60-percent KD run is a timing outlier, so describe the 60-percent average as approximate. Results are from an A30 full-batch workload with data already on-device.

The current evidence answers all four questions
Answers are limited to the models, budgets, seeds, and hardware we tested
The tested pipeline improves efficiency, but it does not outperform the simple degree baseline on accuracy.

preview: Research question | Answer from the current evidence

text: Summarize the four questions. RQ1: modest edge removal can retain accuracy, with degree pruning matching the full graph at 20% removal. RQ2: teacher-guided scoring does not beat the degree baseline in the tested budgets. RQ3: the stronger teacher improves KD results, but matched CE remains ahead. RQ4: sparse graphs and smaller students reduce measured inference latency and peak memory.
The evidence favors a simpler selector so far
A research result can be useful even when the proposed component does not win
Degree pruning has the best accuracy among the tested selectors.
The stronger teacher improves KD, but matched CE remains ahead.
KD tuning is still seed-0 evidence; confirmation is needed before claiming a repeatable gain.
We measured real inference savings, but current results do not show teacher-guided KD beating degree pruning or matched CE.

Target duration: about 2 minute(s).

Do not frame this as a failed project. We tested the central ideas and found where they do and do not help. The systems benefit is measurable. The accuracy results favor degree pruning and CE in the tested settings. The seed-0 KD sweep suggests temperature matters, but the improvement needs confirmation across seeds before we interpret it as repeatable. Also keep the break-even estimate qualified.
Fewer edges can reduce inference cost.
But in our tested settings, simple degree pruning and CE remain stronger accuracy references.

Target duration: about 1 minute(s).

Close the talk in three statements. Edge removal reduced measured inference cost. The larger teacher improved KD transfer over the original teacher. Yet degree pruning and matched CE remained stronger in accuracy under our tested settings. Invite questions on methodology, cost assumptions, and which tradeoff should guide the next experiments.

Q&A after the 40-minute talk.

Open the floor for Q&A. Suggested prompts if the room is quiet: Is the degree baseline a fair enough comparator? How should we weigh accuracy against latency? Which costs belong in the break-even calculation?
